t: Aim and plan of the session
n: In this session we become familiar with the toxicological significance of carboxyhaemoglobin and the methods of analysing it in blood. That is the aim of the session. The plan consists of two parts. The first: the toxicological significance of carbon monoxide poisoning. The second: analysis of carboxyhaemoglobin in blood by chemical and physicochemical methods. In the DVSSM course package this topic is supplemented with quantitative analysis by the UV spectrophotometric method.

By the end of the session students master the conditions for analysing carboxyhaemoglobin in blood by chemical and physicochemical methods. For the work, test tubes, separating funnels, reagents and visual materials will be needed. The session is held in a room equipped with special laboratory facilities.

This is the session map. The plan consists of the significance of carbon monoxide poisoning and the analysis of carboxyhaemoglobin in blood. In the chemical methods, five colour reactions are performed and the poisoned blood is compared with pure blood. The physicochemical methods are spectroscopic, spectrophotometric, photometric and gas chromatographic. In the spectrophotometric method, absorbance is measured at wavelengths of 538 nm and 550 nm, and 550 nm is the isosbestic point. In gas chromatography, 500 µl of blood is taken for methane, and the retention time is 3 minutes.

Carbon(II) oxide, that is, carbon monoxide, is a colourless, odourless and tasteless, fast-acting poisonous substance. It is very poorly soluble in water. Carbon monoxide burns with a bluish flame: 2CO + O2 → 2CO2. Its mixture with air from 16 to 73% can explode. Because it has no smell, poisoning occurs quickly and suddenly. This is why this gas is especially dangerous.

Carbon monoxide is formed when organic substances, coal, gas and other fuel products burn incompletely. Poisoning occurs when a blast furnace malfunctions, when a stove damper is closed too early, or when coal is placed in a sandal. Poisoning also occurs from the carbon monoxide in exhaust gas released because of a vehicle fault. The table gives the content by source: in natural gas 4–30%, in "water gas" 40–50%, and in the explosion of a shell or mine about 30%.

Let us memorise the key numbers for carbon monoxide. The explosive limit in air is 16–73%. The rate of binding to haemoglobin is 300 times that of oxygen, while the release of CO from COHb is 3600 times slower. Death occurs when COHb reaches 70–80%. A concentration of 0.07–0.08% in air is dangerous, and the permissible one is 0.02 mg/l. These numbers form the basis of the topic.

Staying for a long time near a stove, hearth or gas cooker can lead to unpleasant consequences. Malfunction of blast furnaces, closing the damper of a domestic stove too early, and placing coal in a sandal cause poisoning. Natural gas may contain 4–30% carbon monoxide. Therefore, knowing how to use gas correctly is also one of the measures for preventing poisoning.

CO readily combines with haemoglobin to form stable carboxyhaemoglobin: HbO2 + CO → HbCO + O2. As a result, haemoglobin loses its ability to carry oxygen, and the patient dies of oxygen deficiency. The rate of binding of CO to haemoglobin is 300 times that of oxygen. The release of CO from COHb is 3600 times slower than the release of oxygen from oxyhaemoglobin. Therefore the compound formed persists for a long time.

t: COHb level and degree of poisoning
n: Death occurs when COHb in the blood reaches 70–80%. Detection of COHb in the blood proves that the patient was poisoned by carbon monoxide. The table gives the degrees. If COHb is 20–30%, the poisoning is mild. 30–35% is moderate. 35–50% is severe. At 50–60%, strong poisoning is observed: convulsions and loss of consciousness.

t: Forms of haemoglobin in the blood
n: Four forms are present in poisoned blood: deoxyhaemoglobin Hb, oxyhaemoglobin OHb, carboxyhaemoglobin COHb and, in part, methaemoglobin MtHb. Remember: MtHb does not combine with carbon monoxide. Cadaveric lividity is dark red. Owing to carboxyhaemoglobin, the blood becomes dark red, and the liver, kidneys and lungs appear reddened.

t: Elimination from the body and the air standard
n: Carbon monoxide is eliminated from the body only through the respiratory tract. Opinions differ on how long it persists in the body. According to the first opinion, it persists for up to 122 days. According to the second, it cannot be detected after 25–40 hours. Carbon monoxide at 0.07–0.08% in air is dangerous to life, and the permissible concentration is 0.02 mg/l.

t: Principle of detecting carbon monoxide via blood
n: Detection of carbon monoxide in poisoning is based on determining carboxyhaemoglobin in blood by chemical and physicochemical methods. To detect it in an object, the object is crushed, the blood is separated and the composition of the blood is examined. To detect carbon monoxide in air, the air is passed through animal blood and is collected in the blood. This blood is then analysed.

t: General principle of the chemical methods
n: A great many chemical reactions have been proposed for detecting carbon monoxide in blood. In them, the colour changes of poisoned and pure blood are compared. The chemical methods are based on COHb being more stable than oxyhaemoglobin. For a conclusion, the results of several reactions are compared. Remember: relying on only one leads to error.

The first reaction is performed with potassium ferricyanide, the red prussiate. As the reagent, 5 drops of a 1% solution of K3[Fe(CN)6] are taken. Procedure: water is added to 1 ml of blood up to 100 ml, and 5 ml of this is taken. As a result, blood containing COHb does not change its red colour, while pure blood turns brown.

The second reaction is performed with copper sulphate. The blood is diluted with water 1:100, 3 ml is taken, and 3 drops of 10% copper sulphate solution are added. Blood containing COHb keeps its dark red colour. Pure blood turns green.

The third reaction is performed with caustic soda. To 0.5 ml of undiluted blood, 1 ml of 30% caustic soda solution is added. Blood containing COHb does not change its dark red colour; pure blood turns brown. Be careful: in blood in which putrefaction has begun, a bright red colour, that is, haemochromogen, forms even without carbon monoxide.

The fourth reaction is performed with formaldehyde. To 1 ml of undiluted blood, 1 ml of 40% formaldehyde solution is added and shaken well. Blood containing COHb does not change its red colour. Pure blood turns brownish-black after 5–10 minutes. If 20% formaldehyde is added, the colour change is noticeable within 40–60 minutes.

The fifth reaction is performed with lead acetate. To 0.5 ml of undiluted blood, 2 ml of 5% lead acetate solution is added and shaken for one minute. Blood containing COHb keeps its red colour. Pure blood turns brown.

Now we summarise the reagents and volumes. For potassium ferricyanide and copper sulphate, the blood is diluted with water 1:100. For NaOH, formaldehyde and lead acetate, undiluted blood is taken. The reagents: 1% K3[Fe(CN)6], 10% CuSO4, 30% NaOH, 40% formaldehyde and 5% lead acetate. In all the reactions, blood containing COHb does not change colour, while pure blood does.

The chemical methods have limitations. In blood in which putrefaction has begun, a bright red colour, that is, haemochromogen, forms with NaOH even without carbon monoxide. In partly mild poisoning, the reagents give the same result as with unpoisoned blood. When the amount of COHb is small, the method is of no value. Relying on the result of only one reaction leads to error, so several reactions are compared.

The colour table is written in the workbook: blood containing COHb and pure blood are compared side by side. With K3[Fe(CN)6], COHb is red and pure blood turns brown. With CuSO4, COHb is dark red and pure blood is green. With 30% NaOH, COHb is dark red and pure blood is brown. With lead acetate, COHb is red and pure blood is brown. With formaldehyde, COHb is red and pure blood becomes brownish-black after 5–10 minutes.

t: Interpreting the chemical reactions and their limitation
n: Pure blood reacts with the reagents, whereas in poisoned blood there is no noticeable change. However, in partly mild poisoning, the reagents give the same result as with unpoisoned blood. Therefore the chemical methods of examination are of no value for detecting a small amount of carboxyhaemoglobin. That is, these methods give only supporting guidance.

Let us consider additional tests. If unpoisoned blood is diluted with water, a brown colour forms, whereas COHb does not change its dark red colour. If tannin acts on normal blood, a grey substance forms, and the colour of blood containing COHb does not change. A mixture of potassium ferrocyanide and acetic acid gives a brown colour with normal blood. Formalin forms a dirty brown substance with normal blood, whereas blood containing COHb does not change.

In the spectroscopic method, blood containing COHb is examined with a spectroscope, and the Fraunhofer lines in the D and E region of the spectrum are visible. Oxyhaemoglobin gives two absorption bands between the D and E regions: 577–589 and 536–556 nm. Carboxyhaemoglobin forms a spectrum in the regions of 564–579 and 523–536 nm. Under the action of ammonium sulphide, the OHb spectra merge into a single broadened band at 543–596 nm, while the COHb spectrum does not change.

The spectrophotometric method is based on reducing oxy- and carboxyhaemoglobin to deoxyhaemoglobin and measuring absorbance. Three solutions are prepared. Solution A: 1 ml of blood is diluted to 100 ml with phosphate buffer of pH 7.38 or with 0.1% ammonia; the solution must be clear. Solution B: 3–4 mg of sodium dithionite is added to solution A. Solution V: saturated with CO, and 5–7 mg of dithionite is added. Then the spectrum is measured in the range 450–620 nm.

t: Obtaining CO and saturating the blood
n: Now obtaining carbon monoxide and saturating the blood. CO obtained from conc. H2SO4 and formic acid is first passed through 10% alkali; the alkali retains the HCOOH. Then the gas is passed through water, that is, freed from alkali, and directed into the vessel containing solution A. In this process, the oxyhaemoglobin in the blood is completely converted into carboxyhaemoglobin.

t: Comparing solutions A, B and V
n: We compare solutions A, B and V. Solution A: 1 ml of blood without clots is diluted to 100 ml with phosphate buffer of pH 7.38 or 0.1% ammonia; the colour must be clear. Solution B: 3–4 mg of sodium dithionite is added to solution A in the cuvette, and the oxyhaemoglobin is fully reduced to deoxyhaemoglobin. Solution V: solution A is saturated with CO, then 5–7 mg of dithionite is added and it is saturated with CO again.

Once the solutions are prepared, the light absorption spectra of solutions B and V are measured in the range 450–620 nm and plotted on a single graph. Absorbance is measured in two monochromatic beams: 538 nm and 550 nm, that is, at the isosbestic point. The percentage of COHb is calculated by the formula, with the coefficient K = 0.372. The result serves the forensic medical assessment.

Let us consider the spectral characteristics. Deoxyhaemoglobin, that is, solution B, gives one spectral maximum at 557 nm. Carboxyhaemoglobin gives two maxima at 541 and 571 nm. The curves intersect at 550, 565 and 580 nm; these are isosbestic points. Absorbance is measured at two wavelengths: 538 nm, that is, D1, and 550 nm, the isosbestic point D2. The coefficient K = 0.372.

The determination procedure in the ammonia variant is as follows. The blood to be tested is placed in a 100 ml volumetric flask and made up to the mark with 0.1% ammonia solution. The mixture is placed in a 1 cm cuvette, sodium hydrosulphite crystals are added and it is shaken. Absorbance is measured at 538 nm and 550 nm. The reference solution is 0.1% ammonia.

We define the symbols in the calculation formula. R is the carboxyhaemoglobin content in the blood, in percent. D(COHb) is the absorbance at 538 nm of the blood in solution V saturated with CO. D(HbCOHb) is the absorbance at 538 nm of solution B with dithionite added. D(Hbi) is the absorbance of solution B at 550 nm, that is, at the isosbestic point. The coefficient K = 0.372.

The result obtained serves the forensic medical assessment of carbon monoxide poisoning. Detection of COHb in the blood proves that the patient was poisoned by carbon monoxide. Work with blood is carried out with minimal contact with air, away from sources of natural and artificial light. Blood solutions prepared for photometry must be clear.

The identity and amount of methane are analysed mainly by gas-liquid chromatography. 500 µl of blood and 500 mg of minced biomaterial are placed in a penicillin vial and closed with a rubber stopper. The vial is heated in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. The vapour-gas mixture is withdrawn with a syringe and injected into the GLC. Conditions: Svet-110, thermostat 50 °C, vaporiser 150 °C, carrier gas nitrogen, 30 ml/min. The retention time of methane is 3 minutes.

Let us consider a situational problem. Physical evidence: 10 ml of blood. The corpse has pink lividity; in the internal organs the blood is very fluid and scarlet in colour. Circumstances: died by drowning in a bath in a home bathroom. Task: to determine by which poisonous substance the poisoning occurred. The forensic chemical analysis is carried out using the "carousel" table.

Case 24: a crime was committed in the Tashkent region, and organs of 3 corpses burnt inside a car were found. The question is as follows: was the person killed first and then burnt to destroy traces, or burnt alive? Task: to carry out the forensic chemical analysis. The answer table consists of the type of problem, the causes of its occurrence and ways of solving it. If carboxyhaemoglobin is detected in the blood, it is proved that the patient was poisoned by carbon monoxide.

Review questions. What are the sources of carbon monoxide formation, with chemical equations, and the measures to prevent poisoning? Explain the effect of carbon monoxide on the human body and the ways of eliminating it from the body. What are the signs of carbon(II) oxide poisoning? What phenomenon are the chemical methods used to detect carbon monoxide in blood based on? What colour-forming reactions have been proposed for detecting carbon monoxide in blood?

Review questions. What physicochemical properties does carbon monoxide have and by what route does it enter the body? At what amount of carboxyhaemoglobin in the blood can the patient die? What physicochemical methods are used for the qualitative and quantitative determination of carbon monoxide in blood? What processes is the spectrophotometric determination of carbon monoxide in blood based on, and how?

We conclude. COHb is determined by chemical reactions, that is, by the difference in colour, and by physicochemical methods, that is, spectroscopy, spectrophotometry and GLC. The chemical methods are of no value for detecting a small amount of COHb, so several reactions are compared. In the spectrophotometric method, the percentage of COHb is calculated using the absorbances at 538 and 550 nm and K = 0.372.
